Collinder 41 is one of 19 clusters resized in SIMBAD (maintype Ocl) per https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2022/08/aa43146-22/aa43146-22.html and data in J/A+A/664/A66/tablea1 (2 times the radius of the largest FOV value).  Bracken’s sky atlas lists it as aka vdB 19 and types the object as Ref Neb with dimensions of 10’ x 15’.  This is another case of overriding cluster and nebula identifiers in SIMBAD and historical catalogs.  It is listed in Historical NGC (Steinicke’s work) as a cluster but listed in NED as a Nebula with a diameter of 6 arcminutes!  In OpenNGC it is listed as “Cl+Neb” (both) with a diameter of 10 arcminutes.  Aka IC 1985, LBN 758.

Collinder 70 aka Orion’s Belt includes 100 or so stars in the belt.  Diameter varies by catalog.  Collinder’s (1931) dimensions are 250’ x 120’ at 140 degree angle (125 stars), and Lundmark’s are 240’ x 140’ at 125 degree angle (90 stars).  Collinder’s note (pp. B26 – B27, 1931): “Cl. around Belt of Orion. […] This is a very fine cl.  The following stars from HDC are in the belt …” and lists coordinates (in B1900 from the Henry Draper Catalog) that map to Mintaka, Alnilam and Alnitak (delta, epsilon and zeta Orionis), two of them being double stars and all of them type B0, the three main stars of Orion’s Belt.  The 2000.0 coordinates (83.9, -1.083333) are from Archinal and Hynes (2003) who reference works by Brian Skiff in the 1980s and 1990s.  SIMBAD has slightly different ICRS J2000 coordinates (83.875, -1.1) and no angular size or position angle data for this object.  After testing different options, using the Archinal and Hynes J2000 coordinates with Collinder’s dimensions and angle fits best and avoids including sigma Orionis, which may be the center of its own separate cluster.

Collinder (1931) Cr 103 dimensions are Lundmark at 20’ x 20’ vs Collinder at 7’ x 7’.  That is an unusual disparity between their two sets of values and makes me wonder if they were looking at the same object.  Collinder’s note (p. B28) lists diameters from Reinmuth at 16’ and Lundmark at 15’.  Yet, in the catalog entry, the values listed are different from the note.  The remainder of the note states: “Irregular object.  Lk: Clear cut absorption on prec. Side.” Yet the dimensions given are not irregular.  However, the entry Cr 101 is irregular and listed with Lundmark dimensions of 15’ x 6’, with Collinder’s of 12’ x 5’ – both agreeing on a elongation angle of 140 degrees.  I think it likely that the note for Cr 102 is meant to go with the object in Cr 101.  Here adopted the SIMBAD coordinates over RNGC.

Collinder 458: SIMBAD coordinates are in a totally different area of the sky at (81.883, +7.075), listed as alias of Dolidze 21 and no diameter info as of 11/2026 and its source is MWSC (2013A&A...558A..53K) and this seems to be a confusion.  Archinal and Hynes (p. 110, Table 4.1, 2003) list it as primary id of Harvard 21 aka Cr 458 and note “Probably not a real cluster.” But, I think they’re coordinates are off too, just a bit, because there is a formation at the coordinates I have listed here that stands out nearby in a diagonal line with Cr 459 and Cr 461, about the same size and class, looking much more the part than either the SIMBAD or A&H coordinates.  Note there are many small clusters in this region noted by King, Berkeley, Teutsch, Stock, Frolov, etc … and when I do look at the others, King 12 is exactly at the location that jumped out to visually as being the best nearest candidate for Cr 458.  I think the MWSC and A&H missed this one.  Collinder’s alias for Cr 458 is Harvard 21. Using Lundmarks dimensions and angle here because testing shows they map well to the object’s size and shape: 5’ x 3’ at 80 degrees.  Lundmark’s note (p. B44, 1931) says “At end of dark lane.  Bona fide cluster.”  Yet Collinder’s note for the same object contradicts saying “Doubtful object.” Go figure!
